entries.title: Unity Catalog Metric Views, now in Power BI: one unified, governed semantic layer for all your reporting and AI
entries.summary: Organizations want a single, trusted definition of their business semantics. Revenue,...
entries.content:
Define semantics once in Unity Catalog and publish them directly to Power BI semantic models

by Toussaint Webb, Joanna Zouhour, Chris Eubank and Jade Wang

  • Make Databricks the home of your semantics: Keep metric views, relationships, Pages, and other modeling metadata in one governed place with Unity Catalog Semantics, not scattered across different tools.
  • Model once, consume across AI and BI: Define metrics and data models once in Unity Catalog metric views and publish them directly to Power BI semantic models from Catalog Explorer or a Power BI task. Receive consistent results across Power BI, AI/BI dashboards, and Genie.
  • Stay governed and in sync: Unity Catalog access controls stay in place with DirectQuery, and Power BI task orchestration keeps Power BI models up-to-date as your UC metric views change.

Organizations want a single, trusted definition of their business semantics. Revenue, margin, and active customers should mean the same thing in every report, notebook, and AI application. When they don't, business users and AI agents read the same data differently and reach different answers. Finance and sales show different revenue numbers, teams lose trust in their reports, and decisions get made on the wrong numbers. Unity Catalog metric views, part of Unity Catalog semantics, solve this by enabling customers to define business KPIs once in Databricks, in an open, governed semantic layer that sits on top of the lakehouse.

At the same time, many of these organizations rely on Power BI as the front end for their business users. Often, organizations have thousands of PowerBI workspaces each with its own Semantic Models, creating a governance and unification nightmare. Furthermore, when each team builds its own metrics and relationships in Power BI, the same logic lives in many places. Reports drift apart, and every definition change means updating each copy.

Customers have told us they want both: Databricks as their unified, open semantic layer, and Power BI as their front end. With Publish to Power BI, they can now have both. Every Power BI report uses the same governed UC metric views as AI/BI dashboards and Genie, so teams work from consistent numbers. Business users can build self-serve reports and explore metrics across any dimension without waiting on a data team to model data or write DAX. Data teams maintain one definition in Databricks instead of many copies across systems. Publish on demand from Catalog Explorer, or add a Power BI task to a Lakeflow Job to keep metric views and semantic models in sync in production.

With Publish to Power BI or a Power BI task, you can connect Unity Catalog metric views to a Power BI semantic model. Each metric view becomes a table in the model. The metric view’s dimensions (aka Fields) become columns and its measures become DAX measures.

Power BI queries the metric view itself (as if it was a table). The metric view stays the source of truth, and joins defined in the metric view run in Databricks. Joined dimensions, such as campaign channel or region, show up in Power BI as ordinary columns, so you don't have to rebuild table relationships in Power BI.

For example, a marketing team needs to track campaign performance and decide where to shift budget. They define a campaign_performance metric view in Unity Catalog with dimensions such as channel and region and measures such as total spend, total revenue, and return on ad spend (ROAS). When the team publishes the metric view, those dimensions and measures arrive in Power BI like this:

A marketing analyst can then build a Power BI report that compares ROAS by channel and region, and see the same numbers the team gets in AI/BI dashboards and Genie. If the team later changes what counts as total_revenue they update the metric view once, a Power BI task in their pipeline republishes it, and every Power BI report picks up the new definition.



Because Power BI queries the metric view, it will soon be able to benefit from metric view materialization too. Metric view materialization is a performance optimization that pre-computes results without changing how metrics are calculated. When Power BI sends a query, Databricks will serve it from a matching materialization for faster results. If no materialization matches, the query runs against the metric view as usual. Either way, the metric definitions, DAX measures, and results are identical.

Additionally, with Lakehouse//RT + DirectQuery, Power BI reports get real-time performance, directly on your governed lakehouse data. Lakehouse//RT runs on your managed Delta tables, so there's no separate serving system to copy data into or manage. It also enforces the same Unity Catalog row filters, column masks, and ABAC policies, so reports get faster without giving up governance.

With DirectQuery, every query honors Unity Catalog access controls and security policies, and lineage stays connected to the metrics your teams already use in AI/BI dashboards, Genie, and Databricks Lakehouse.

When a metric view changes, we make it easy to keep Power BI up to date. Using Power BI tasks in Lakeflow Jobs, you can publish your metric views to the target semantic model as a step in your data pipeline, on a schedule or right after upstream tables refresh. Updated measures, new measures, and new dimensions flow into Power BI automatically, so reports stay aligned with the metrics layer without manual rework.

Publish to Power BI covers the metric definitions most teams use day to day:

  • Data modeling: Define your data model directly in metric views, including joins and relationships, dimensions, measures, and other semantic metadata, and let Databricks handle the computation automatically without manually duplicating logic in Power BI.
  • Measures: Standard aggregations (SUM, COUNT, AVG, MIN, MAX, MEDIAN, STDDEV, VARIANCE), distinct counts, ratios, filtered measures, and measures composed from other measures.
  • Window measures: Current, offset, and trailing window measures.
  • Metadata: Descriptions and display formats including currency, decimal and percentage settings carry over to Power BI field properties.
  • Storage modes: DirectQuery (the default) for live queries against Lakehouse/RT or Databricks SQL, and Import mode for loading data into Power BI.
  • Publishing mechanisms: Use Publish to Power BI in Catalog Explorer to publish metric views on demand in a few clicks. Use Power BI tasks in Lakeflow Jobs to automate publishing as part of your data pipeline, so metric views and semantic models stay in sync in production.

Publish to Power BI is available in Private Preview (documentation). Work with your account team to test out the preview. 

Once enabled, you can publish in three easy steps:

  • Prepare the metric view(s): Add any measure inputs as dimensions and make sure every field is named.
  • Publish: In Catalog Explorer, click Publish > Publish to Power BI, sign in with your Power BI credentials, and choose a target workspace. When you're ready for production, add a Power BI task to a Lakeflow Job to automate publishing, ensuring your Power BI semantic model stays in sync with your metric view.
  • Validate in Power BI: Open the semantic model and confirm that the metric view appears as a table, dimensions appear as columns, and measures appear as DAX measures.

Together, these capabilities make Databricks the home of your semantics. Define your metrics once in Databricks, keep Power BI models in sync using Power BI tasks, and use the same governed definitions everywhere, including the Power BI reports business users already rely on. Every team and use case works from one open, governed platform.

What is a governed semantic layer, and why do BI and AI agents need one?

A governed semantic layer is one place where business metrics and shared dimensions like revenue, country, and active customers are defined. Every BI tool, notebook, and AI agent then uses those definitions the same way. Unity Catalog Semantics is that layer in Databricks. It brings together metric views, relationships, and other modeling metadata in Unity Catalog. It's open, you can query it with SQL, and it inherits Unity Catalog access controls and lineage. That's why a Power BI report, an AI/BI dashboard, and a Genie One agent all return the same ROAS number.

How do you give AI agents and BI users the same business definitions?

Build business definitions once in a shared semantic layer that is accessible by all of your tools. Don't encode it separately in each BI tool or agent prompt. With Unity Catalog metric views, Genie One and Agent Bricks agents read the same governed definitions that Power BI reads through Publish to Power BI. When a definition changes, every consumer gets the update. 

Should metrics live in Power BI semantic models or in Unity Catalog?

Keep the metric definitions in Unity Catalog. A Power BI semantic model primarily serves Power BI. It is hard to access from external BI tools or AI agents, requiring the same metric to be rebuilt in every tool. Publishing metric views to Power BI turns each measure into DAX automatically, so Power BI users keep their reports, while maintaining a single governed definition for AI and other use-cases.

Does Power BI query the metric view or the underlying tables? 

The metric view. Only the measure expressions are translated to DAX, and they reference the metric view's dimensions. The metric view stays the source of truth, and joins and calculations run in Databricks.

What does the published semantic model look like?

Each metric view becomes one table. Its dimensions become columns and its measures become DAX measures. Because joins are defined once in the metric view, joined dimensions show up as ordinary columns and no Power BI relationships are needed. For example, SUM(amount) becomes SUM('sales_metrics'[amount]), and MEASURE(a) / MEASURE(b) becomes DIVIDE([a], [b]).

What happens when a metric view changes? 

To keep models in sync automatically, add a Power BI task to a Lakeflow Job so publishing updates runs on a schedule or after upstream tables refresh.

Is access still governed by Unity Catalog? 

Yes, with DirectQuery. Every query honors Unity Catalog access controls and security policies. In Import mode, data is loaded into Power BI, so access to that copy follows Power BI permissions. 

Do changes made in Power BI sync back to Unity Catalog? 

No. To ensure unified and governed semantics, publishing only goes one way, from Unity Catalog to Power BI. If you edit a published measure in Power BI, that edit isn't written back to the metric view. To change a governed metric, update the metric view in Databricks and republish, or create a Lakeflow Job with a Power BI task to update the Power BI semantic model on a schedule.

entries.title: Databricks' Commitment to European Sovereignty
entries.summary: Over a Decade of Investment in EuropeDatabricks has been building in Europe since...
entries.content:
• Data has never been more valuable, and European organizations want to harness it boldly and responsibly, with partners they can trust. Across the region, organizations are building AI and analytics on their most sensitive data under European control. Frameworks like DORA, NIS2, the EU AI Act and the EU Data Act, along with emerging proposals such as the European Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA), reflect that shared ambition.
  • We’re expanding our sovereignty commitments so customers can innovate with confidence on the cloud of their choice. Databricks will launch on the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (AWS ESC), and we’re committed to ensuring Azure Databricks meets EU sovereignty requirements and customer expectations.
  • This builds on years of partnership with European customers to secure, govern and get more from their data. Our track record includes GDPR leadership and support for the EU Data Boundary, and we’ll keep deepening our sovereign capabilities as our customers’ ambitions grow.

Databricks has been building in Europe since our first regional launch in the Netherlands in 2017. Today we serve thousands of European enterprises across 17 European cloud regions. Our growing European team of more than 2,000 employees works from 15 offices in Europe, including several engineering hubs. In addition, European customers can now contract directly with a Databricks European Union (EU) entity, making procurement simpler for customers that require a European counterparty.

That investment has always been driven by a specific philosophy: customers should control where their data lives, how it's protected, and who can access it. Our platform is built so customers decide where their data is stored, and who holds the keys that protect it. Databricks is the engine that processes data, not a vault that holds it. Combined with open formats and a multi-cloud architecture, this means sovereignty never has to come at the cost of lock-in. We are extending our partnership by committing to build three new regions in Europe, Azure Italy, Azure Spain and AWS European Sovereign Cloud (AWS ESC).

Meeting strict compliance and residency requirements isn’t new territory for us. Databricks was an early leader in GDPR readiness and among the first to build functionality such as “right-to-be-forgotten” deletion management. We’ve continued to evolve our platform alongside regulations and customer expectations, including support for the EU Data Boundary, so customer data is stored and processed where customers choose. For highly regulated workloads, Databricks already operates under some of the world’s most rigorous frameworks.

Today, we’re seeing growing interest from European customers in stronger sovereignty controls. To help them continue innovating on Databricks while their data and production environments remain under European control, we’re expanding our sovereign cloud commitments across both Azure and AWS.

Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud brings sovereignty controls to the Azure regions. Databricks and Microsoft are working together to extend those controls to Azure Databricks, including operational oversight, personnel controls, and transparency measures designed to meet the expectations of European regulators and customers. Databricks is classified as a regional service on Azure and has been Azure EU Data Boundary compliant since EUDB launched.

We're committing to making Databricks natively available on the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. AWS ESC is a physically and logically independent cloud, operated within the EU, that AWS brought to general availability in early 2026. It's designed to give European organizations the highest levels of operational autonomy, resilience, and data protection, and it's a natural home for the most demanding sovereignty workloads. Bringing Databricks to AWS ESC means customers won't have to choose between sovereignty and a modern data and AI platform.

True digital sovereignty is a journey, not a switch. Our immediate focus is bringing Databricks to the Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud regions and AWS European Sovereign Cloud, and we’ll keep adding controls that strengthen our sovereign offering over time, including support for any open standard compatible storage so customers can keep data on-premises or in European clouds.

As the sovereign landscape evolves, we’ll keep listening to our customers and partners and evaluating additional sovereign options based on what they need. Our commitment stays the same: customers should control where their data lives, how it’s protected, and who can access it.

Forward-looking statement: This post describes plans and timelines that are subject to change and do not represent a commitment to deliver any specific functionality by a specific date.

entries.title: Accelerate GPU training on Unity Catalog tables with UCDataset
entries.summary: GPUs are usually the most expensive part of any training run, and most teams can't...
entries.content:
by John Spencer, Milan Stefanovic, Bruce Fontaine and Tejas Sundaresan

  • Accelerate training times by 10x and reduce compute costs with UCDataset, a native data loader currently in beta that streams data directly from Unity Catalog tables to your GPUs
  • UCDataset plugs directly into standard PyTorch training loops and automatically handles multi-GPU data sharding without requiring custom code
  • By reading training data directly from Unity Catalog, you can ensure governance is applied automatically

GPUs are usually the most expensive part of any training run, and most teams can't keep them busy. The bottleneck usually isn't the model. It's getting data from where it lives to the GPU fast enough - and every second those chips sit waiting, you're burning both time and money.

Today we're releasing the Unity Catalog Dataset (UCDataset) in Beta on AI Runtime. UCDataset is a native PyTorch data loader that streams Unity Catalog tables directly to every GPU in your training job, with no exports, no copies, and no custom loader code.

On simulated production workloads, UCDataset cut training time by 10x compared with reading an exported Parquet copy of the same data.

Most training data for your models already lives in Unity Catalog tables. Getting it into a distributed training job means picking one of three workarounds, and each one costs you time and money:

  • Slow, tedious exports before every run: The most common pattern is to export the table to Parquet (or another shard format) in a volume before every run, then point a dataset at the files. You pay to store a second copy, it goes stale the moment new data lands, and it falls outside Unity Catalog lineage.
  • Pulling the whole table into memory doesn’t scale: Reading the table into pandas with toPandas() works for small tables and fails on large ones. It also lands everything on one node, which doesn't help a job that trains on 32 GPUs.
  • Streaming through a warehouse is slow: Warehouses weren't natively built to feed GPUs and without optimization will get throttled when many GPUs read at once.

Then there's the loader itself. Every GPU and every worker needs its own balanced slice of the data. Teams spend time building this by hand, and a subtle bug can mean the model trains on duplicated or skipped rows without anyone noticing.

The result: expensive GPUs sit idle, training takes longer than it should, and ML engineers maintain data plumbing instead of improving models.

UCDataset makes Unity Catalog tables a first-class data source for distributed PyTorch training. You describe what to read (a table, the columns you need, and a row filter) and UCDataset streams training-ready batches to every GPU. Benefits include:

  • Built for speed: UCDataset reads the table's files directly from cloud storage, so nothing sits between your data and your GPUs. It splits the matching rows evenly across every GPU and data loader worker.
  • Train on the lake, not a copy: Point it at the live table. Filters and deletion vectors apply as the data is read, and the next run picks up newly appended rows automatically.
  • Governed end to end: Training jobs read data as the identity that runs them, and Unity Catalog permissions apply exactly as they do everywhere else on Databricks.

We benchmarked UCDataset on a simulated production workload, streaming a 300 GB feature table across 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs to train a recommendation model and saw on average a 10x improvement in training time compared to loading data directly from Parquet.

How to use it:

Say a team keeps user and item features with a click label stored in a main.recsys.ctr_features table. New impressions land on the table every day. They want to train a click-through-rate model on 16 GPUs across two nodes, straight from the table.

1. Describe what to read and create the loader. In train.py, pick the table, keep the labeled training rows, and select only the columns the model needs. The filter is applied as the table's files are read, so rows that don't match never reach your training code. UCDataset already yields whole batches, so wrap it in a standard PyTorch DataLoader with batch_size=None.

2. Train and launch on two nodes. Train with a standard PyTorch DDP loop. UCDataset gives each of the 16 GPUs its own share of the matching rows, so there's no sampler or sharding code to write. Describe the job in workload.yaml, which starts train.py with torchrun on every node, and run it with the AI Runtime CLI:

To train on more GPUs, change num_accelerators in workload.yaml. The training code stays the same. The complete train.py and workload.yaml, with a sample table to try them on, are in the AI Runtime cookbook: Click-through-rate model on a Unity Catalog table.

Install the package from PyPI. In a notebook, run 

%pip install databricks-uc-dataset
.

UCDataset is available in Beta on AI Runtime. To try it:

  • Read the docs: Load Unity Catalog tables into PyTorch with UCDataset
  • Start from a working example: cookbook recipe
  • Talk to your account team, we would love to hear your feedback.

For unstructured data stored in Unity Catalog volumes, use UCVolumeDataset to stream files with local caching. While UCDataset handles structured tables, we are also expanding it to support multimodal training via the FILE type - allowing you to train on images, audio, and documents directly from a table. The Beta reads Delta tables in Unity Catalog.

UCDataset (Unity Catalog Dataset) is a native data loader that streams Unity Catalog tables directly to the GPUs in a training job. It's available in Beta on Databricks AI Runtime. You choose a table, the columns you need, and UCDataset delivers training-ready batches with no export step or custom loader code.

UCDataset keeps GPUs busy by reading a table's data files directly from cloud storage, without an exported copy in between. It splits the matching rows evenly across every GPU and data loader worker, so each GPU reads only its own share.

No. UCDataset reads the live table in Unity Catalog, so there's no export step and no second copy to store or keep in sync. It applies your filter and the table's deletion vectors as it reads, and each new run picks up rows appended since the last one.

Yes. On AI Runtime, training jobs read data as the identity that runs them, and Unity Catalog permissions on the table apply. Because the job reads the governed table directly, there's no exported copy to secure separately. In the Beta, UCDataset can't read tables that have row filters or column masks.

UCDataset reads Delta tables registered in Unity Catalog, including tables with deletion vectors.

entries.title: Turn buying signals into pipeline with Sendoso gifts in Genie One
entries.summary: From insight to action in Genie OneAI agents are only as useful as the actions they can take...
entries.content:
Ask Genie One which accounts are gaining traction, approve a gift that builds on that momentum, and track what each send influenced.

by Max Child and Allison Bennett

  • Sendoso's MCP server brings gifting and direct mail into Genie One, so business teams can turn an intent signal from their own data into a previewed, approved gift in one conversation.
  • It is installed from Databricks Marketplace as a governed MCP Service in Unity Catalog. Unity Catalog controls who can use it, and Unity Gateway sets which calls need approval and logs every call.
  • Gift history lives in the same workspace as pipeline data, so teams can report on the deals each gift influenced and manage gifting like any other investment.

AI agents are only as useful as the actions they can take. Genie One lets business teams ask questions of governed data in plain language. The next step is acting on the answer in a way that's governed and measurable, without exporting a list or logging in to another tool. Partner MCP servers in Databricks Marketplace close that gap, and Sendoso's is a worked example: a Databricks admin connects it once, and every Sendoso tool becomes available where your data already lives.

Sendoso is a gifting and direct mail platform with tens of thousands of gift options, eGifts, branded kits, custom swag and physical gifts. Its AI suggests gifts, researches recipients and drafts notes, and its MCP server brings that into Genie One, next to the data that shows who to send to and why.

Gifting is worth the effort because other channels are crowded: Sendoso's 2026 Digital Fatigue Report found 84% of buyers are fatigued by cold calls and 83% by marketing emails.

The signals that show who deserves a gift often live in Databricks already. Acting on them meant exporting a list, logging in to a separate tool and rebuilding context by hand.

  • Spot the signal in a dashboard or report.
  • Export a list.
  • Log in to a separate gifting tool.
  • Rebuild the account context by hand.
  • Pick a gift, write a note, and send it.
  • Weeks later, try to match the gift back to the pipeline in a spreadsheet.

By the time the gift went out, the buyer had often moved on, and connecting it to outcomes meant manual spreadsheet work.

Try it yourself: get the Sendoso MCP server on Databricks Marketplace →

Here's what happens in the video (the account and data are illustrative):

1. Find the moment in your own data: The user asks Genie One which target accounts spiked in intent this week and have no gift history. Genie One answers from an intent table in the workspace. The top result is Northwest Robotics, a sample account: intent on gifting automation is up 3x, and the VP of Revenue Operations has viewed the pricing page three times.

2. Turn the signal into a personal gift: The user asks Sendoso to act on it. Genie One brings in the account context from Databricks, and Sendoso searches its gift catalog for something that fits. It proposes a gift and a note built from the reason the account spiked.

3. Preview, then approve: Nothing is charged at this stage. The user reviews the gift, the recipient and the note, and approves it.

4. Track it, or cancel before it ships: After the send, the user gets a confirmation showing what was sent, what the note said, and a send ID. The send ID tracks the gift in Sendoso, and the gift can be canceled until it ships.

5. Show leadership what the gifts did. Gift send history sits in a table in the same workspace, so the user can ask Genie One to summarize the sends for executives.

Because the signal, the send, and the send history sit in the same governed workspace:

  • Teams target accounts their data shows are active and can act the same day.
  • Send history sits next to the pipeline data, so teams can report on what gifts influenced using their own attribution model.
  • Sendoso's budgets and approvals apply to every send. Unity Catalog controls who can trigger them, and Unity Gateway can require approval on each call.

$2M+ pipeline from eGifts,

$2.3M+ pipeline and 12 hrs/week saved,

Samsara, Procore and Talkdesk have already shown what targeted gifting can do. In Genie One, teams can run those plays on their own intent data and measure the outcomes they influence.

Team Signal in Databricks What Sendoso does in Genie One
Sales (SDRs and AEs) Intent spike or stalled deal A gift and note matched to the buyer's interest
RevOps and GTM leaders Gift history next to pipeline An executive summary of gifts and pipeline influenced
Customer success Health score drops A recovery gift instead of a generic check-in
Demand gen and marketing Lead crosses a score A small eGift within a spending limit
Field and event marketing Event attendance A thank-you or meeting-booking gift
Customer and partner marketing Milestones or renewals An appreciation gift, tracked like any channel
Developer Relations MVP or product fan gifts An appreciation gift for software adoption to build a product fanbase

Business users don't need to configure anything. A Databricks admin connects it once:

  • Install: the admin installs the Sendoso MCP server from Databricks Marketplace as a governed MCP Service in Unity Catalog. Once it's in place, users add the Sendoso connector directly in Genie One.
  • Govern: Unity Catalog permissions control who can use it. The admin then scopes what agents can call through Unity Gateway, which can also require approval for high-risk actions and logs every call for auditing. Sendoso's own budgets, spending limits and campaign approvals apply to every send made through the MCP server, just as they do in the Sendoso app.
  • Respect roles: every tool runs as the signed-in Sendoso user, so it only sees what that user can see and only does what their role allows.

For requirements and step-by-step configuration, see the full setup guide: Using Sendoso in Databricks Genie One →

  • Ask your Databricks admin to install the Sendoso MCP server from Marketplace.
  • Check that your signals, such as intent, engagement, CRM and health scores, are in Databricks.
  • Pick one play from the table above and run it in Genie One.
  • Review the results, then roll out to the next team.

For more plays, see Sendoso's companion post.

How do I measure the ROI of gifting with Sendoso and Databricks? With send history in the same workspace as pipeline, renewal and engagement data, you can apply your team's attribution model to measure the meetings, pipeline and renewals gifts influenced, and compare that with what you spent. Ask Genie One for the results in plain language.

What is an MCP server in Databricks, and what does Sendoso's do? An MCP server exposes an external system's tools to agents. In Databricks it's installed as a governed MCP Service in Unity Catalog, and Unity Gateway controls which tools agents can call. Sendoso's MCP server makes its gifting tools available inside Genie One, so users can find a gift, send it, track it and see what it influenced without leaving Databricks.

Who is this for? Any team that sends gifts or direct mail: sales, customer success, RevOps, demand gen, field marketing, and customer or partner marketing. Users work in plain language in Genie One, with no code.

Can an agent do more than the user who is using it? No. Every tool runs as the signed-in Sendoso user, so it only sees what that user can see and only does what their role allows. Unity Gateway policies can restrict it further.

Is anything charged before I approve a gift? No. Sendoso first shows a preview of the gift, the recipient and the note. Nothing is charged until the user approves it, and Sendoso's budgets and campaign approvals apply just as they do in the Sendoso app.

Can I track or cancel a gift after it is sent? Yes. After a send, you receive a confirmation that includes a send ID, which you can use to track the gift in your Sendoso instance. You can cancel the gift up until it ships.

How do I set it up? A Databricks admin installs the Sendoso MCP server from Databricks Marketplace as a governed MCP Service in Unity Catalog and scopes what agents can call through Unity Gateway. Users then add the connector directly in Genie One.

entries.title: Read, don't copy: replacing file feeds with OpenSharing - Part 2 (How to Implement)
entries.summary: Many data-sharing architectures begin with a familiar pattern: A provider exports...
entries.content:
What the recipient actually does with a shared table

by Jordan Soldo

  • OpenSharing exposes a Delta table via an open protocol, so recipients can read it live rather than ingesting from scheduled file or API exports.
  • It removes the per-recipient export jobs, file tracking, and reconciliation that are required by file and API feeds.
  • Recipients read the shared table as a checkpointed incremental stream, with row-level inserts, updates, and deletes received through Change Data Feed.

Many data-sharing architectures begin with a familiar pattern:

  • A provider exports a file on a schedule.
  • The file lands in a bucket or is transferred through an SFTP endpoint.
  • The recipient detects the new file, loads it, deduplicates it, and tracks what has already been processed.
  • Updates and deletes require additional conventions or reconciliation jobs.

Part 1 of this blog described why a shared table can be a better alternative to a recurring file or API feed. Now let's look at what the recipient actually does with that table.

This walkthrough focuses on Databricks-to-Databricks (D2D) sharing. The recipient has a Unity Catalog enabled Databricks workspace and accesses the shared table through a shared catalog. The provider shares the table with its history, enabling the recipient to use it as a Structured Streaming source. We'll come back to Databricks-to-Open (D2O) sharing later in the post.

A Delta table keeps an ordered history of every change made to it. OpenSharing exposes that table over an open protocol without copying it. The data stays in the provider's storage, and the recipient reads it live.

On the recipient side, you point a Structured Streaming reader at the shared table. Spark records how far it has read in a checkpoint, so each run picks up only the changes made since the last one. Tracking "what's new since I last looked" becomes the engine's job, running over governed data with lineage and access control intact.

Let’s take an example: a retailer maintains a live orders table and shares it with an external recipient running Databricks. Instead of receiving a nightly CSV, the recipient can query the shared orders table directly. If the recipient needs a local copy for analytics or downstream workloads, it can incrementally materialize the data into a Delta table. The setup happens once and is split between the provider and recipient.

Create the source table with Change Data Feed on, then publish it in a share WITH HISTORY. History is what makes the table an incremental source. Without it, the recipient only gets a static snapshot. Enabling Change Data Feed (delta.enableChangeDataFeed) is optional for the main incremental read below. Turn it on only if you plan to use the upserts and deletes path later. If you're on Databricks Runtime 19 or above, you can skip the property and rely on automatic Change Data Feed, which computes row-level changes at query time for tables with row tracking enabled and works with Databricks-to-Databricks OpenSharing.

Register the recipient by their sharing identifier, then grant the share:

Do note that CREATE SHARE and CREATE RECIPIENT require metastore-level privilege, not just workspace admin.

The share now shows up as a provider in your metastore. Mount it as a catalog, and you can read it like any other table.

With the share mounted as shared_in, reading is handled by Structured Streaming.

Trigger.AvailableNow processes all currently available, unprocessed data using one or more micro-batches and then terminates. This makes it a good fit for scheduled incremental jobs. Instead of a fixed schedule, you can also configure the job with a table update trigger on the shared table, so the job runs only when the provider commits new data. It is recommended to store the checkpoint in durable cloud storage such as UC Volumes.

Note: This example reads a shared table through Delta Sharing, so it uses ignoreChanges. If you stream directly from a regular Delta table, newer Databricks runtimes use skipChangeCommits for append-only processing.

To prove it's actually incremental, run the stream once against an initial set of rows. Run it again after you have new rows on the provider. The target table's commit history will show two streaming writes:

Version

Operation

Operation Metrics

2

STREAMING UPDATE

numRemovedFiles: 0, numOutputRows: 200, numOutputBytes: 2307, numAddedFiles: 1

1

STREAMING UPDATE

numRemovedFiles: 0, numOutputRows: 1000, numOutputBytes: 4958, numAddedFiles: 1

0

CREATE TABLE

{}

The second run wrote 200 rows, not 1200. The checkpoint tracked the last version read, so the run pulled only the new ones.

ignoreChanges is suitable for this incremental landing pattern, but it may re-emit rows and does not propagate deletes. If downstream consumers need inserts, updates, and deletes, read the shared table’s Change Data Feed instead:

When a new customer is added, the provider does not need to create a new SFTP endpoint or implement a new export job. The provider grants the recipient access to the share. The recipient uses the same general pattern while keeping its own target tables and downstream business logic separate. The operational difference is significant:

  • The provider manages a single governed source table instead of a separate export.
  • Access is managed through the share: D2D recipients use permissions on the shared Unity Catalog, while D2O recipients use the applicable OpenSharing credential flow.
  • The recipient retrieves data from table history rather than keeping track via custom files or timestamps.
  • Backfills can use historical table versions rather than requiring the provider to recreate the old files.
  • Change Data Feed gives the recipient explicit insert, update, and delete events when that behavior is required.
  • Both parties have a clearer boundary: the provider owns the shared data product, and the recipient owns its downstream processing.

Everything above works because the recipient runs Spark on Databricks, which is what unlocks checkpointed streaming and CDF. Other recipients (pandas, BI tools, Snowflake) connect through OpenSharing with a credentials file instead of a metastore sharing ID.

If they run OSS Spark, the read is the same spark.readStream code through the delta-sharing connector. Without Spark, there's no continuous stream, so they pull changes by version range:

A useful first project does not need to solve every sharing scenario. Start with one regular Delta table and one recipient.

Before implementing the stream, answer these questions:

  • Is the recipient D2D or D2O?
  • Does the recipient need a snapshot, incremental reads, or row-level CDC?
  • Does the share include history?
  • Is CDF enabled if updates and deletes must be propagated?
  • Which Databricks Runtime or OpenSharing connector version will the recipient use?
  • How will the recipient handle retries, duplicates, deletes, and schema changes?
  • Who owns monitoring and support after the share is in production?

Once those answers are clear, validate the smallest possible end-to-end flow: create the share, read an initial snapshot, write a new row, update a row, delete a row, and confirm that the recipient sees the expected results.

That is the practical shift OpenSharing makes possible. Instead of building a new transport and ingestion workflow for every customer, you can establish a governed data-sharing contract and let each recipient consume the data through the path that fits its platform.

New to OpenSharing? Start with What is OpenSharing? and Create shares for OpenSharing, then stand up the minimal end-to-end flow above against one table and one recipient.

entries.title: Read, don't copy: replacing file and API feeds with OpenSharing - Part 1 (The Why)
entries.summary: If you ingest data from your customers over SFTP or APIs, you have probably asked...
entries.content:
Simplify how you ingest customer data, without the pipeline upkeep, backfill pain, and duplicate storage of traditional feeds

by Jordan Soldo

  • Traditional customer feeds get expensive as you scale: Every SFTP drop or API pull means another pipeline to monitor, fragile incremental loads, backfills that depend on your customer, and a duplicate copy of their data to store.
  • Read the customer's table in place instead of copying it: With OpenSharing, you can follow changes on the tables your customers share through streaming or change data feed, without tracking what's been processed yourself.
  • Sharing gets easier for your customers: Adding you as a recipient is just a grant on a table they already maintain, and audit logs record every time you access their shared data.

If you ingest data from your customers over SFTP or APIs, you have probably asked yourself at least one of these questions.

  • Can I pull only what changed, instead of reprocessing whole files?
  • Can I get new data as soon as my customer writes it, instead of waiting for the next file drop?
  • Can I backfill months of data without asking my customer to re-export it?
  • Can I show my customers exactly when their data is being accessed?

The answer is yes, but not with the patterns most teams still rely on.

Data engineering has come a long way, but customer ingestion has barely changed. Most teams still use SFTP file dumps, API pulls, or managed connectors. Each of these patterns works, but each also carries hidden costs that quietly add up as you take on more customers.

Ideally, you should be able to use a table's own version history to incrementally pull just the new data, and simply read the table your customer already maintains, with no SFTP to stand up and no per-customer connector to babysit. You would also get the freshest data, because as soon as your customer writes to the table, it becomes immediately available to you and every other recipient.

OpenSharing does exactly that. It is an open protocol for reading a table in place, built on open table formats such as Delta Lake and Iceberg. Because the protocol is open, you don't even need to be on Databricks to read what your customer shares.

None of this happened overnight. It began with file-based feeds, as they were a simple ingestion pattern: your customer simply drops a file via SFTP or into a bucket, and your job picks it up. Following that, APIs arrived when customers demanded something fresher than a nightly file. Instead, you could pull changes on your own schedule while the customer maintained an API endpoint. Then came managed connectors. This was the natural next step once custom-coding each feed connected to an API or SFTP stopped scaling, leading to new customer onboarding becoming configuration rather than code.

While each has its place, the real problem is what they quietly cost you once you start maintaining these pipelines.

Most hidden costs stem from managing every pipeline, since each customer has their own quirks that can introduce failures. SFTP file dumps need to handle cases where your customer uploads something other than the agreed-upon files into the SFTP server. On the other hand, APIs hide their own set of failures.

Let's use an endpoint that returns data as an example. Calling the endpoint often demands passing a time parameter, where, in turn, it returns data. It is this parameter that can cause pain, as failing to keep track of the last timestamp can cause your copy of the data to drift. For managed connectors, that connection can still fail, and you lose a ton of flexibility.

In backfill scenarios, you feel the most pain. Let's say you find a bug and need to reprocess months of data. If you aren’t currently storing the raw data you ingest, you end up needing to work with your clients. For files, you may need to ask a customer to re-export months of data. In the case of APIs, you end up having to re-poll them for data in chunks, likely hitting rate limits or other blockers.

In all of this, you are keeping track of the last data you processed for each customer. However, if your bookkeeping drifts, you end up either duplicating rows or missing a potential batch, and can potentially create a silent failure where you end up spending countless hours debugging.

The pain is felt not only by you, the consumer, but also by your own customers. Providing this data means building and babysitting an export, with its own schedule, format, and failure mode. The customer also loses all visibility into whether you've even accessed it, and has to trust, with no way to verify, that no one else has queried it. Lastly, both parties incur storage costs because they maintain a duplicate of this data.

OpenSharing addresses several of these problems because you are no longer taking a copy of your customers' data. Instead, you read the customer's table directly in place through the open protocol.

Shared tables can also expose a change data feed. This means that whenever your pipeline runs, it can read the feed to know which records have been created, deleted, or even updated. So now the table you used to maintain to track what has already been processed becomes a checkpoint your pipeline manages for you.

In addition, if a customer shares the entire historical table with you, you can resolve backfill situations smoothly. In these cases, you can simply query the data you need to backfill. OpenSharing provides direct access to the table; you do not need to pay for storage to duplicate this data, and you access the freshest data whenever you query it.

Your customer gets the better end of this, too. Instead of building and babysitting an export just to feed you, they share a table they already keep, and adding a recipient is just a grant. On top of that, reading their tables does not slow down their systems, because you read straight from cloud storage with your own compute rather than querying their database. Lastly, with Databricks system tables, they can see when a recipient queries a shared table, replacing the trust they previously extended on faith with an audit trail they can actually read.

We set out to tackle the problems that come with traditional customer ingestion. By utilizing OpenSharing, you can read a table in place, allowing you to pull only what changed, see new data the moment your customer writes it, turn backfills into a query instead of a favor you ask for, and give your customer an audit trail of every access.

See Part 2, for setting up OpenSharing with a customer end to end, from creating the share to reading changes incrementally in your own pipeline.

entries.title: How public sector organizations can govern AI at scale
entries.summary: Every government CIO has the same mandate right now: adopt AI, move faster, and do...
entries.content:
Unity Gateway centralizes compliance and cost controls so agencies can adopt AI with confidence

• Unity Gateway provides clear answers on cost, compliance, and data residency let public sector teams move AI projects forward.

• Agencies already using Unity Catalog can govern AI the same way they govern data, controlling model access, capping spend, and tracking every request.

• Databricks manages data residency for its hosted models by geography, giving compliance teams a documented answer on where AI requests are processed.

Every government CIO has the same mandate right now: adopt AI, move faster, and do more with less. As coding assistants make development teams more productive and AI agents open up new ways to serve citizens, the cost of waiting grows every day for agencies.

But public sector organizations operate in a different reality than commercial enterprises. Before a single AI model or agent gets called, someone has to answer a set of security and compliance questions that most AI tools or inference providers weren't designed to address. It’s not that public sector organizations are slow to adopt technology; the stakes are just different. The governance requirements that come with the responsibility of handling citizen data, defense information, law enforcement records, and public funds are not optional.

Until recently, meeting those requirements meant saying no to AI, or at least saying "not yet." The tools available didn't give governance, budget, and compliance teams what they needed to say yes.

That's starting to change.

Here's what it looks like on the ground. A digital services team at a public sector organization starts using third-party coding agents, such as Codex and Claude Code, to help developers work faster. Developers love them, but then come the governance questions: Who has access to which models? Why is AI spend climbing so fast?

The compliance team asks where the data is going. It turns out the third-party coding agent platform is routing requests to infrastructure in another country. For an organization handling sensitive operational data, that's a problem.

The budget office asks about costs. No one can say how much the tools are costing or which teams are driving the spend. Response times are slow and unnecessary tokens are being used because requests are traversing infrastructure that was never optimized for the use case.

The result is predictable: the compliance team can't sign off, the budget office can't plan for it, and the AI project stalls. Not because teams don’t need AI, but because no one can answer the basic governance questions.

This pattern repeats across agencies and geographies. The specific regulations vary, whether it's GDPR, FedRAMP, or national sovereignty frameworks, but the underlying dynamic is the same. Teams want to use AI. Governance teams want to say yes. But the tools in the middle aren't giving either side what they need.

The public sector organizations that are making real progress on AI share a common trait: they solved governance before they scaled adoption. They didn't bypass the governance questions. They found a way to answer them centrally, so every team didn't have to figure it out on their own.

That's the role Unity Gateway plays within Databricks.

No single model fits every mission, so agencies need choice.

  • A citizen services assistant answering permit and tax questions around the clock handles high volumes in many languages, so it needs a model that responds quickly and costs little per request.
  • A fraud unit tracing patterns across benefits claims needs a model that can reason through complex evidence, and it can only run where that data is allowed to go.
  • A records office extracting details from scanned legal filings needs a model that reads documents and images, not just text.
  • A critical agency application is built on an obsolete code base, so updating it requires a frontier model that excels at complex coding tasks.

Choose one model for all three, and the agency either overpays for routine questions or under-serves its most demanding work. Governance has to make room for the right model for each mission while keeping data, users, and budgets under control.

What Unity Gateway gives governance and budget teams is straightforward. The organization controls which AI models, coding agents, MCPs, and AI tools are available and to whom. Teams get day-zero access to the latest frontier and open-source models, while administrators decide which models to enable and who can use them. New models don't become available to every user by default.

For example, at a revenue agency, that means an investigations unit can use AI on taxpayer records while access stays limited to the investigators authorized to work those cases. Spending limits and hard caps can be set by user, team, or use case, and every request is tracked and attributable. Compliance policies, including content guardrails and access controls, apply at the platform level to every AI interaction, regardless of which team or application initiates it.

Beyond setting spending limits, Unity Gateway helps organizations reduce AI costs with Smart Routing, which directs tasks to more cost-effective models while maintaining quality. For an agency modernizing legacy systems on a fixed budget, that means routine coding tasks go to lower-cost models, stretching the budget further without slowing developers down.

For organizations with strict data residency requirements, governance also has to cover where AI requests are processed. A national health service applying AI to patient records, for example, has to be able to show regulators where that data goes. Databricks manages data residency for its hosted foundation models by geography, and account admins can require that these requests be processed within their workspace's geography. Compliance teams get a clear, documented answer on where those requests are processed.

And because Unity Gateway supports models from multiple providers, open-source models, and external endpoints, teams aren't locked into a single vendor. They can use the best model for each task, while the governance team retains full visibility.

When organizations move their AI workloads to Unity Gateway, the dynamic that was stalling adoption reverses. Developers get access to the models they want through Databricks' infrastructure without each team needing to self-govern. The governance team gets a single view of AI activity across models, agents, and tools, with unified traces that capture requests, token usage, costs, and tool activity.

For the benefits agency, that means leaders can see that AI tools for processing claims are being used heavily and at a reasonable cost, so they can expand those tools to more caseworkers and get benefits to people faster.

The governance requirements that were blocking AI adoption become the unified foundation that makes it possible. When the compliance team has confidence that AI usage is visible and managed, and the budget office can see exactly where spending is going, saying yes to AI gets much easier.

Governments around the world are investing in AI while tightening data protection and sovereignty requirements. From citizen services to national security, the agencies that move fastest will be the ones that can match each mission to the right model, with the right controls.

Unity Gateway is how Databricks helps public sector organizations get there. It meets agencies where they are, with existing data governance in place, and adds AI governance on top. No parallel system. No multi-year implementation. Just the controls that public sector leaders need to move forward.

Want to learn more?

  • Follow Databricks for Public Sector on LinkedIn
  • Visit the Unity Gateway webpage

Do we need new infrastructure?

No. Unity Gateway is built into Databricks, allowing organizations to centrally manage AI access, security, and costs without deploying or maintaining a separate AI gateway or AI governance solution.

Can we control which models our teams use?

Yes. While Unity Gateway provides day-zero access to the latest AI models, administrators can control which models are enabled and who can use them. Organizations can approve models and manage access by user, group, or team, so teams can adopt new AI capabilities without compromising governance.

Can we set spending limits?

Yes. Budgets and hard spending caps can be set by user, team, or use case. Every request is tracked.

Does this work with multiple model providers?

Yes. Unity Gateway supports models from multiple frontier model providers, open-source models, and external endpoints.

Can we keep AI processing within our geography?

Yes. Account admins can require that requests to Databricks-hosted foundation models be processed within their workspace's geography. If a model isn't available in that geography, admins can choose to allow processing elsewhere.

entries.title: Real-time fraud detection with Feature Views
entries.summary: Real-time fraud detection depends on three kinds of features: what a customer did...
entries.content:
Follow a single $900 payment from an Apache Kafka stream to a live fraud score, with code for streaming, on-demand and point-in-time correct features on Databricks.

  • Feature Views define fraud features once and reuse them for point-in-time training and online scoring, reducing data leakage and training-serving skew.
  • Rolling windows catch payment bursts, a 30-day Sawtooth baseline captures normal spend and an on-demand feature scores each payment against that baseline.
  • One materialize_features() call creates managed streaming pipelines into the Online Feature Store on Lakebase, with sub-200ms feature freshness.

Real-time fraud detection depends on three kinds of features: what a customer did seconds ago, how they normally spend and how the current payment compares. Those features have to be computed the same way for model training and for live scoring — otherwise data leakage and training-serving skew quietly erode model quality. Feature Views, part of Databricks Feature Store, address this. You define each feature once, and that definition produces both point-in-time training data and the managed pipelines for online inference.

A $900 payment may be routine for one customer and unusual for another. When it arrives, a fraud model has only a moment to decide whether it looks normal, needs review or should be blocked. Approving a fraudulent transaction can cost the customer money. Blocking a legitimate one disrupts their payment experience and erodes their trust in the platform.

The transaction alone doesn't tell the whole story. The model also needs to know how this customer normally transacts and what they did seconds, minutes, days or weeks ago. During training, features must use only information available when each payment occurred. During live scoring, they must reflect recent transactions quickly enough to catch suspicious activity. If the two paths implement the logic separately, small differences between them creep in.

This walkthrough follows that $900 payment from a Kafka stream to a fraud score served by Model Serving, with code at each step. The central idea is that one feature definition, driving both training and serving, gives you point-in-time correct training data and consistent online features. You don't build a separate pipeline for each path.

A Feature View is a Databricks Feature Store definition that specifies a feature's source, entity keys, time semantics and transformation. The same definition computes historical values for training and drives the managed pipelines that keep features fresh for serving. One API covers batch, streaming and on-demand features. Unity Catalog governs their definitions, permissions and lineage.

Two failure modes motivate this design:

  • Training-serving skew happens when a feature is computed one way in training and another way in production. At inference time, the model then sees inputs that don't match what it learned from.
  • Data leakage happens when training data includes information that wasn't available at prediction time. Point-in-time correct features prevent it by using only events that happened before the moment being predicted.

Feature Views bring streaming feature computation into the same data science workflow as historical training and live scoring. You can evaluate features against past transactions, then use the same definitions to keep customer context fresh for live decisions.

The goal is to flag suspicious payments as they arrive without raising false alarms on legitimate ones. On its own, the $900 payment may look harmless. But if it's the 10th payment in five minutes, it could be part of a suspicious burst. Any delay in recognizing that burst gives someone with access to a compromised account more time to make additional payments.

A Fraud Detection application built with Databricks Apps processes a stream of financial transactions. Each event includes a customer ID, amount, payment type, timestamp and origin and destination countries. The application sends each transaction to a Model Serving endpoint. It then displays the transaction's risk score alongside live transaction volume, flagged transactions and country-to-country flows.

The model combines three kinds of context:

  • Recent activity: a five-minute transaction count and a 10-minute total amount, computed with RollingWindow, capture how often the customer is paying and how much they're spending.
  • Spending baseline: a 30-day average and standard deviation, maintained with SawtoothWindow, describe the customer's typical payment amount and how much it varies.
  • Transaction details: the current payment's amount, payment type and origin and destination countries give context for the decision.

The architecture has a historical path for training and an online path for inference. Both start from the same feature definitions in Unity Catalog. The historical path reads the Stream's ingestion table to build point-in-time training sets. The online path materializes aggregates to the Online Feature Store, where Model Serving reads them at request time.

Before deciding which features to serve, you can test alternatives against historical transactions. Does a five-minute transaction count give a stronger signal than a 15-minute count? Does comparing the current amount with the customer's spending variability help beyond using their average alone?

In this example, customer transaction events arrive as Kafka streams. A registered Stream holds the connection, schema and ingestion settings, and a StreamSource references it to compute real-time features. Kafka topics don't retain enough history for model training. Databricks therefore manages an offline copy of the stream in an ingestion table. For training or backfilling an online store, Databricks calculates historical values from the ingestion table and uses the live Kafka feed for the most recent data.

On ingest, 

transformation_sql
reshapes nested fields from the Kafka value payload into the schema the features need. The projection becomes part of the source definition, so you don't deploy a separate preprocessing pipeline. For our payment, the Kafka value payload contains:

The demo uses 

demo_user_id
alongside 
customer_id
to keep the customer histories of different app users separate.

We define the five-minute count with 

RollingWindow
. The companion notebook includes imports, configuration, and the full source projection.

You can inspect its historical values in a notebook with 

compute_features(features=[recent_transaction_count])
. The 10-minute total uses the same source and keys, with Sum over a 10-minute RollingWindow.

A Sawtooth window is a long-lookback aggregation whose oldest boundary advances in daily steps. It combines batch-computed history with streaming updates for recent activity. For our $900 payment, 

SawtoothWindow
adds a 30-day spending baseline to the short rolling windows. Both kinds of window keep recent activity fresh. Because the Sawtooth window's oldest boundary moves daily rather than continuously, its effective lookback is slightly longer than 30 days. The baseline uses the built-in 
Avg
, 
StddevPop
and 
Count
aggregations on payment amounts over the same Sawtooth window.

Databricks starts a managed ingestion pipeline when a Stream is created and keeps incoming events in its ingestion table. If you also need events from before the Stream existed, 

StreamBackfillSource
lets you supply your own history during Stream setup. Once the table covers the full lookback, a new Sawtooth feature can use it right away instead of waiting 30 days for events to accumulate.

An on-demand feature is computed at request time by combining values from the scoring request with stored features. Comparing a live transaction against a customer's historical baseline is a common way to spot abnormal behavior. In Feature Views, inference-time information is represented with a 

RequestSource
— here, 
transaction_amount
from the application's request.

Two customers can both average $300 per payment but spend very differently. With standard deviations of $100 and $600, the same $900 payment sits six standard deviations above one customer's average and only one above the other's. The model combines this comparison with recent activity and payment details to estimate fraud risk.

The Sawtooth aggregations maintain the 30-day average and standard deviation. The on-demand feature combines them with the current amount to calculate 

(current_amount - average) / standard_deviation
. We implement this calculation as a Python UDF registered in Unity Catalog:

The feature definition uses registered upstream Feature objects. 

FeatureViewSource
brings together the current amount and the three 30-day statistics, and 
CustomUDF
invokes the function:

When there isn't enough usable history, the function returns zero as a fallback. A separate indicator lets the model tell that fallback apart from a true zero, which means the payment matches the customer's average. The same derived feature is evaluated against historical inputs during training, and against the current request plus retrieved statistics during inference.

During feature development, you can inspect feature definitions in a notebook with 

compute_features()
. This works for derived features whose inputs come entirely from historical source data. For request-dependent comparisons such as 

amount_deviation
, use 
create_training_set()
 instead, which supplies the current payment fields from labeled examples. The Unity Catalog function must exist, but feature definitions can stay unregistered while you test candidates.

This lets you check whether a feature improves the fraud model's offline performance before deploying it for live scoring. For example, you can compare models with and without 

amount_deviation
on later held-out payments. These experiments run on batch compute over transaction history, so you can evaluate each candidate without setting up online materialization. Once you've selected the features, register their definitions and materialize the rolling and Sawtooth aggregations for serving.

Each historical training example needs features computed as of that payment's timestamp. For our $900 payment at 10:00 AM, the five-minute count should include transactions from 9:55 AM up to, but not including, 10:00 AM. A count retrieved at 10:03 AM could include a payment made at 10:02 AM, which wasn't available when the original payment was scored. That's data leakage: the model learns from future activity, and its offline performance looks better than it really is. Feature Views use each example's customer keys and timestamp to compute the correct historical window from events in the Stream's ingestion table.

After registering the selected features, 

create_training_set()
builds the model's training data. The labeled DataFrame supplies the customer keys, event time, current payment fields and 
is_fraud
. This excerpt selects the walkthrough's registered features, including the 30-day baseline, and uses rows before a chosen cutoff for training:

Keys and timestamps select customer history but are excluded as model inputs. Request fields feed the feature computations; the classifier uses the resulting named features. Later rows form a validation set using the same definitions.

We train a random-forest classifier and evaluate average precision and ROC AUC on the latter. We then log the model through the Feature Engineering client. Passing 

training_set=train_set
records the feature dependencies that serving will need:

Moving the above selected features into live scoring requires pipelines to maintain streaming aggregates, process historical data, and keep the online store up to date. Building and operating these pipelines adds months of data engineering work beyond developing the fraud model. With Feature Views, the registered feature definitions drive this process: a call to 

materialize_features()
creates managed pipelines that make the aggregations available in Databricks Online Feature Store, powered by Lakebase.

The streaming path uses Spark Real-Time Mode (RTM) to process incoming events continuously and update rolling aggregates as they arrive.

We materialize the rolling and Sawtooth aggregations. For the 30-day Sawtooth baseline, Databricks maintains the historical portion with batch computation and the recent activity with streaming. The two are merged on read into a single feature, and 

StreamingMode()
manages this hybrid path without a separate batch call. Check both materialization paths in Catalog Explorer before serving. The Sawtooth guidance recommends waiting two full days before production use. 

RequestSource
supplies values from each scoring request, and derived features are computed on demand. Once the model is deployed, the application sends the customer keys and current payment fields to its endpoint. Model Serving retrieves the latest customer features and evaluates the on-demand deviation, then passes the inputs to the fraud model. Here's our $900 payment in the app's request format, using the SDK call from the scorer:

The app sends 

event_time
in this request, but online lookup uses the latest available customer features, not a historical snapshot selected by that timestamp. In this demo, the app scores each payment before publishing it to Kafka. That keeps the current payment out of its own history, which matches the training window's exclusion of that payment. Feature updates and scoring still run asynchronously, so other events may be in flight when the next payment is scored.

The endpoint returns a probability in 

fraud_probability
and a flag in 
fraud_prediction
. The application stores scored transactions in Lakebase for the dashboard.

Production fraud models raise governance questions: which models use a feature, where it comes from and who can read it. Unity Catalog brings feature definitions, permissions and lineage together to answer them. MLflow records which features each model uses, and Model Serving uses those dependencies when it handles an inference request.

Feature privileges control the lifecycle:

  • CREATE FEATURE
    controls registration.
  • READ FEATURE
    grants access to feature metadata.
  • MANAGE
    authorizes operations such as materialization.

Feature privileges don't replace the 

SELECT
permissions needed on the source or materialized tables for training and serving.

In Catalog Explorer, Feature Views appear under Functions, with their definitions, source links, materialized tables and status. Streaming materializations link to their system-managed Lakeflow pipelines for inspection. Materialization tags let teams attribute pipeline or job compute costs to a specific team or project.

Our $900 payment now has context: recent activity, a longer-term baseline and the current request. Three practices made that possible:

  • Define once, use twice. Shared feature definitions for training and serving reduce the training-serving skew that comes from separate implementations.
  • Compute point in time. Training windows that exclude future events prevent data leakage and keep offline metrics honest.
  • Let the platform run the pipelines. Materialization and online lookup are managed, so the work stays focused on choosing better fraud signals.

The same patterns go beyond this walkthrough. 

LastN
keeps sequences such as the destination countries of a customer's 10 most recent payments, which helps models spot changes in payment routes. Batch features can also use lifetime aggregations to summarize an entity's complete history.

For a closer look at the infrastructure behind sub-second streaming freshness, read How Databricks Feature Store serves features with sub-second freshness. For implementation details, see the docs for the Feature Views API, materialization and exploring Feature Views in Unity Catalog.

What are Databricks Feature Views?

Feature Views are a capability of Databricks Feature Store for defining ML features once and using them for both training and production. Each definition specifies a source, entity keys, time semantics and a transformation. The same API covers batch, streaming and on-demand features, and Unity Catalog governs them.

How do Feature Views prevent data leakage when training a fraud model?

Feature Views compute each training example's features as of that example's timestamp. For a payment at 10:00 AM, a five-minute transaction count includes payments from 9:55 AM up to, but not including, 10:00 AM. This keeps future activity out of the training data, so offline performance isn't inflated.

What is training-serving skew and how do Feature Views reduce it?

Training-serving skew occurs when features are computed one way for training and another way for live inference. Feature Views reduce it by using one registered definition for both historical computation and online materialization. Teams don't have to reimplement feature logic for production.

Can Feature Views compute features from Kafka streams?

Yes. A registered Stream holds the Kafka connection, schema and ingestion settings, and a 

StreamSource
references it in feature definitions. Databricks keeps an offline copy of the stream in an ingestion table for training and backfills. Real-Time Mode updates streaming aggregates as new events arrive.

How are real-time features served to a fraud model in production?

Calling 

materialize_features()
creates managed pipelines that keep aggregates current in the Online Feature Store, powered by Lakebase. When the model is logged with 
log_model()
and deployed on Model Serving, the endpoint retrieves the latest customer features and computes on-demand features from the request. It then returns a fraud probability.
