entries.content:
How to keep your app fast and reliable as usage grows

by Bruno Tafur and Tushar Madan

  • Scaling Databricks Apps starts before any code: agree on how quickly the app should respond and how many users it must support at peak times, then send heavy work to the right service. App compute serves the UI and coordinates calls.
  • Code that scales keeps the app responsive while waiting for services, uses per-user caching and keeps state recoverable. Soft state can be rebuilt; hard state lives in Lakebase or Unity Catalog tables so any instance can rebuild a session.
  • Use load tests and telemetry to choose the instance size, worker count and instance count. Budget Lakebase connections, and add compute to meet measured demand and availability targets.

Congratulations, you've built an app on Databricks Apps, and it's gone from a couple of users to hundreds or thousands across your organization. Your users want it to respond fast and stay up. And your boss may not love having to pay for XLarge compute across a stack of instances.

How do you make an app that runs fast, stays up and handles growing demand? The intuitive answer is more compute, but that only helps once you know where requests spend their time and whether the app is built to scale: its framework, async code and ability to run on several instances, so the platform can easily scale it up or out.

In this guide, we walk through how to scale Databricks Apps across four stages: design; build; test and deploy; and operate (Figure 1).

The focus of this guide is primarily application performance and resiliency at scale; it does not cover deployment automation or performance optimization and scaling of other Databricks services that may interact with the app.

Figure 1: Four stages of scaling a Databricks App.

Good scaling decisions start before any code is written: agree what users need from the app, then decide where the work will run and where the data will live.

Before choosing an architecture, it helps to pin down how much load the app has to handle and what a good experience looks like. We suggest agreeing two main targets:

  • Performance: how quickly must key actions respond? We recommend end-to-end latency targets based on a percentile, such as p95, which captures the slower experiences that an average will not show. Include UI rendering, and treat cold starts separately. For streaming AI responses, time to first token matters too.
  • Scalability: how many users are active at peak, how often do they use it and how much growth should the app support? Busy periods such as month end belong in this estimate because that's the load the app has to handle within its latency and error-rate targets.

Alongside these, decide which work must survive a restart and check that critical dependencies can support that. This shapes how you split state and how many instances you run.

Next, sketch a few user journeys, such as opening a dashboard or submitting a question. For each action, note the services it calls, roughly how many calls it makes and which depend on each other, how fast it should finish and how stale cached data can be. These assumptions shape the architecture and the first test targets. Once a prototype runs, you can measure the real calls and revise them.

Suppose a retailer gives its 2,000 store managers an app to check stock, backed by Lakebase. During the busiest hour of Black Friday, 200 of them are using it at once. If each makes two stock checks per minute on average, that is 400 checks per minute. If each check executes three SQL statements against Lakebase, expect 1,200 statements per minute, or 20 per second on average during that hour.

This estimates query rate, not concurrency. Test bursts and growth, validate against live usage, and budget connections separately (see "Budget the connections to Lakebase").

App compute is there to serve the UI and coordinate calls, not to do the heavy lifting. We recommend sending each kind of work to the service built for it (Figure 2). For long-running calls, run the work in the background, for example as a job, and let the UI poll for status or receive streamed updates, rather than holding one request open until it finishes.

If the app needs to run code it doesn't control, such as code written by users or generated by an agent, don't run it in the app. Run it in Databricks Sandbox, an isolated environment that can start from a custom image, so its CPU and memory use stays off the instances serving users.

Figure 2: Where each kind of work runs and where the state lives.

When more people use your app, you can add capacity in two ways: scale up (vertical scaling) by moving to a larger compute size, which gives each instance more CPU and memory, or scale out (horizontal scaling) by adding instances to share the request load. With heavy work running outside the app, what usually limits it is how many requests it can handle at once.

For example, in the Black Friday case, each stock check is light, but checks from 200 store managers can arrive together in bursts. More instances spread those requests, and a larger instance helps if the app can use the extra cores, typically by running more workers. An app that keeps a large reference dataset or model in memory hits a different limit. A larger instance gives it the memory it needs; adding instances doesn't help, because each instance loads its own copy. You can start on Medium and let the load test later in this guide show which you need.

The framework is harder to change later, so it's worth choosing now. Databricks Apps runs apps built on Python or Node.js and you aren't limited to the frameworks below. For most new apps, we recommend AppKit, the TypeScript SDK that 

databricks apps init
and the Databricks agent skills use by default. Caching, telemetry, retry logic and error handling come built in, giving you a starting point for several practices in this guide. AppKit runs one Node.js process per instance by default, so the simplest way to scale is by adding instances.

If you already have an app, or your back end needs Python:

  • JavaScript front end with an API back end (FastAPI, Flask or Express): keep UI state in the browser and make server-side state recoverable across workers and instances. Python back ends can run several workers per instance, for example with Uvicorn or Gunicorn. Node.js back ends run one process per instance by default, so scale them by adding instances.
  • Streamlit or Gradio frameworks: good for data and AI tools built quickly in Python. Streamlit runs as a single process, and both depend on instance-local session handling, so test session continuity during restarts and scaling. For apps that must scale across instances with seamless recovery, prefer one of the approaches above as these frameworks are not recommended.

Whichever you choose, if it keeps session state in server memory, it's worth testing what happens when a session moves to another instance before you scale out.

Most Databricks Apps keep some state in memory, and that's fine as long as you know which parts you can afford to lose. A useful first step is to list what each session holds and what must survive a restart, then split it into soft and hard state:

What it is Soft state Hard state
What it is Temporary working data, kept for speed or context The source of truth, kept durably
Examples In-memory context, caches, work in progress Business records, checkpoints, saved preferences
Where it lives Usually instance memory or local disk, tied to one instance Lakebase or Unity Catalog tables, available to every instance
If it's lost Rebuilt from hard state when possible Must survive restarts and failures, within your recovery needs

How that split works depends on the kind of app:

  • AI agent: keep conversation context, tool outputs and plans in soft state while the loop runs, and save a checkpoint after each meaningful step.
  • Workflow app: stream or poll in-progress status to the UI and save each completed step.
  • Dashboard: keep filter values, reference lists and small datasets in memory, and save user preferences and saved filters as hard state.

Figure 3: When a session moves, another instance can rebuild it from hard state.

Databricks Apps keeps each user on the same instance on a best-effort basis (session affinity) and rebalances sessions when needed, so any per-user cache your app keeps locally usually stays available. Restarts, failures and scaling changes can still move a session, so another instance must be able to rebuild it from hard state (Figure 3).

With targets and an architecture in place, the next step is code that holds up under load, including when a session moves or an instance stops.

We recommend turning on telemetry from the start, so the data is there before you need it. App telemetry writes logs, traces and metrics to Unity Catalog tables through OpenTelemetry. Once it's enabled for an app, logs arrive automatically, but traces and metrics need instrumentation.

You should create custom spans around SQL, database, model and API calls to show where the time goes. Record caught exceptions on the span as well, so they show up in your traces. Trace and request IDs then let you follow one user's requests across instances. For example, a span around a SQL call:

Most apps spend their time waiting on another service: a SQL query, a model call, an external API. With blocking calls, each wait holds an execution slot for the whole call. A handful of slow calls can exhaust that capacity. That's why async handlers matter for I/O-heavy work. When handlers await model and database calls, one worker can keep serving other requests while it waits, as long as those calls are non-blocking. Your traces and system metrics will show when this applies: if most of a request's time is spent in SQL, model or API spans, and latency rises with concurrent users while CPU stays low, requests are likely queuing behind blocking calls.

Even with async, one request can still be slow if it runs its queries one after another. Start independent queries together (for example, with 

asyncio.gather
or 
Promise.all
), so the request takes close to as long as its slowest query. It's also worth capping how many run in parallel, so one request can't flood the warehouse or database. Often it is better to combine queries than to run N+1 queries, where the app fetches a list and then runs one more query per item: a 
join
or an 
IN
clause does the same work in one or two.

A cache speeds up an app, but it can also leak data: an app-level cache doesn't enforce Unity Catalog permissions, so a shared cache can show one user another user's data. Scope cache keys by the user's verified identity and the query parameters, and by session where needed; never key on an identity the client sends without verifying it. Share cached data only when it's identical for everyone. For shared entries many users read at once, let one request refresh an expired entry while the others wait, so they don't all hit the warehouse together. AppKit's cache, for example, deduplicates concurrent cache misses within each instance.

Putting the soft-state and hard-state design into practice comes down to a few recommendations:

  • Persist anything that must survive a restart or deployment. Memory alone is fine for disposable caches, but not for work users cannot afford to lose.
  • Checkpoint wherever you wouldn't want to repeat the work, and make steps idempotent so a retry is safe.
  • Make sessions portable, so any instance can rebuild them from hard state (Figure 3). Reload only what you need, and cache it to avoid repeated reads.
  • Browser apps get session affinity automatically. For stateful API clients, send a stable 
    X-Routing-Key
    header and key it on whatever owns the soft state. Pick a key specific enough to spread load, such as a conversation or user ID rather than a tenant ID. The client sets the header, so use it only for routing, never to decide who the user is.
  • Expect database connections to drop too. They drop when the database restarts or fails over. Reconnect with bounded backoff and jitter, so instances don't all reconnect at once and cause a connection storm. Before retrying a write, check the database to confirm it didn't already go through.
  • Keep the startup light. Every restart, deployment and new instance pays for loading models or datasets, warming caches and opening pools before it can serve traffic. Avoid large installs and blocking external calls at startup, and load heavy resources only when needed.

When you redeploy an app, Databricks sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL if the app hasn't exited within 15 seconds. That window is for final checkpoints. Important work should already be saved during normal operation.

As an example, with FastAPI, Uvicorn finishes open requests before running the lifespan cleanup. 

save_in_progress_sessions()
stands in for your own function that saves unfinished work:

This assumes an async pool (for example, psycopg's 

AsyncConnectionPool
). The Apps-to-Lakebase tutorial uses a synchronous pool, which you close without 
await
.

Set Uvicorn's 

--timeout-graceful-shutdown
below 15 seconds (for example, 10) so a long-running request can't eat the checkpoint time, and test shutdown with your own workload. AppKit's Lakebase plugin closes its pools on shutdown; any custom checkpointing still has to fit in the same window.

Figure 4: System metrics during a stepped load test: latency jumps at the last step while CPU and memory stay below their limits.

Before launch, a load test will help you turn your estimates into decisions closer to reality: the instance size, the workers per instance and the instance count.

We recommend load testing before production, using real user journeys at your expected peak. A tool such as Locust reports requests per second, latency percentiles and the failure rate at each step, and the test passes or fails on the latency and error-rate targets you agreed for the key actions. While the test runs, the app's built-in System metrics show requests per minute, latency, and CPU and memory against their limits, so you can see which limit the app reaches first (Figure 4).

Ramp up concurrent users in steps until throughput stops increasing or latency and error rates break your targets. It's worth trying several instance sizes and worker counts, because a bigger setup isn't always faster. We also suggest testing recovery in a test environment: stop and start the app, not just redeploy or change the instance count during a run, then check whether users can continue, how long recovery takes and whether any work was lost. For agent apps, the load-testing guide walks through testing once with a mocked LLM to measure the app's own throughput, then with the real model for end-to-end latency.

The load generator itself can be the bottleneck: it can run out of CPU or connections first, and authentication errors or rate-limit responses can look like slowdowns. What counts is sustained successful requests within your latency target, not a brief spike.

The load test should also show whether the services behind the app keep up. If the warehouse starts queuing or a model endpoint throttles, scale that service, not the app.

Databricks Apps offers three sizes: Medium (the default, up to 2 vCPUs and 6 GB), Large (up to 4 vCPUs, 12 GB) and XLarge (up to 12 vCPUs, 48 GB). The right one depends on which limit your app hits first, so start on Medium and let the load test show you:

What the load test shows Likely cause What to do
Slow requests with low app CPU The app is waiting on something behind it, or blocking calls are holding workers Keep the size. Fix the query, warehouse, connection pool or blocking calls first, and check per-process CPU too: one maxed-out core can look like low CPU overall
CPU near the limit, server runs several workers (for example, FastAPI with Uvicorn) The app can use more cores Move to Large
CPU near the limit, single-process app (Streamlit, or AppKit by default) Profiling shows the work bound to one core Add instances. A larger size only helps if the app can use extra cores, for example, through worker threads or native libraries
Memory near the limit Large datasets or models held in memory Move up for memory: Large doubles Medium, XLarge gives 48 GB in one instance
Recovery test: the app goes down when its only instance restarts No spare instance to take over Add instances, not a larger size

Workers are server processes within each instance. For Python servers that support this model, you set the count at startup (for example, 

uvicorn --workers 2
), and it applies per instance.

A single worker can leave the CPU idle, but extra workers also compete for CPU and memory. In the benchmark from our load-testing guide, Medium did better with two workers than with four, and Large delivered roughly 2.2x Medium's throughput. Treat the documented starting points, two workers on Medium or eight on Large, as a first guess: the benchmark mocked the LLM and was CPU-bound, and a real app that mostly waits on model calls may get more out of extra workers. Choose the count from your own load test, with the real model.

With horizontal scaling, you set the instance count yourself. The default limit is five instances per app, and your Databricks representative can raise it if load testing shows you need more. Size the count for expected peaks and growth. The app keeps serving while the count changes, and compute cost scales linearly with the instance count. If you're converting an existing app, try it on a duplicate first.

For higher availability, we recommend at least two instances, with enough capacity to handle peak load after losing one: if the peak needs two instances, run three. Extra instances protect against an instance failing, not against problems in the services behind the app.

For a Databricks App that connects to Lakebase with OAuth, we recommend starting with an app-side connection pool on the database's standard (non-PgBouncer) connection string. It reuses connections and fetches fresh OAuth credentials as it opens new ones, as the Apps-to-Lakebase tutorial shows for Python. Set the pool timeout to leave enough time for the query itself before the request deadline.

Those connections add up, so budget them before adding instances or workers. With one pool per worker, the upper bound is instances × workers per instance × maximum pool size: five instances with eight workers and a pool maximum of ten can open up to 400 connections. Add other clients and any connections the app opens on users' behalf, then compare the total with the database's documented limit, leaving headroom for deployments, when old and new versions run side by side.

On-behalf-of user (OBO) queries need identity capacity. This means each user who queries Lakebase as themselves needs their own Postgres role, and Lakebase allows 500 roles per branch. For larger user bases, decide early which queries really need per-user access. Adding instances doesn't change this limit. Where group-level permissions are enough, a Postgres role for a Databricks group lets its members connect with their own OAuth tokens, so one role covers the whole group.

For horizontally scaled apps, Databricks updates one instance first and the rest after it succeeds, so the app keeps serving. It's still worth checking after each deployment that the app is healthy and sessions recover. Keeping the code in Git means you can roll back by redeploying a known good tag or commit. During a rollout, old and new versions run side by side, so keep database and checkpoint formats readable by both, and don't drop fields the previous version needs until you're sure you won't roll back.

After launch, the work becomes a loop: find the slowest step, fix it and measure again. That's why we keep telemetry on in production. On horizontally scaled apps, the Live view in the Logs tab shows one instance at a time; with telemetry enabled, App Telemetry Logs shows all of them.

When something is slow, trace the request end to end (Figure 5).

Figure 5: Where a request spends its time and the main bottlenecks.

These are the symptoms we see most often, and where they usually point:

Symptom Where to look Likely cause What to do
Slow first request after an idle period or a deployment Insights tab System metrics and traces in app telemetry Cold start: app startup, or a service waking from idle Check app startup time and whether Lakebase or the SQL warehouse stops when idle, and keep startup light
Slow requests with low app CPU Insights tab System metrics and traces in app telemetry The app is waiting on something behind it, or blocking calls are holding workers

Check traces for query, warehouse or connection-pool delays before adding app compute

For single-process apps, consider that low overall CPU can still mean one core is maxed out
App CPU or memory near the limit Insights tab System metrics The app itself is the bottleneck, or it holds too much in memory Profile CPU-heavy work, move large state out of memory, then see the guidance in "Pick the instance size"
Timeouts waiting for a database connection App logs and Lakebase metrics Pool contention, long transactions or database connection limits Inspect connection usage and transaction duration, then adjust pools or database capacity within the connection budget
Users lose work or see errors during deployments or rescaling Insights tab System metrics Soft state that can't be rebuilt, or a shutdown that doesn't finish within 15 seconds Checkpoint important work, make sessions rebuildable on any instance, and test shutdown with your real requests and streams

We recommend planning alerting as part of setup: decide who is notified when the app goes down, and feed 

app_status.state
and 
compute_status.state
from the Apps API into your monitoring tool. App status alone doesn't prove users can work, so also check a representative user journey, with its latency and error rates. Allow for brief state changes during deployments when you set thresholds.

Scaling Databricks Apps means sizing the whole request path, not just the app server: set latency and peak-load targets, send heavy work to the service built for it, keep state recoverable, and let load tests and telemetry decide where capacity goes. Add compute when the measurements show you need it, not as a first reaction.

To go further, read how to build production-ready data and AI apps with Databricks Apps and Lakebase. For more details, see Best practices for Databricks Apps and Logging and Monitoring for Databricks Apps in the documentation. For architecture patterns by app type, such as internal tools, AI copilots and agentic workflows, watch Building Better Apps and Stateful Apps for Thousands of Users from Data + AI Summit 2026.

How do I scale a Databricks App?

Scale it in four stages: design, build, test and deploy, and operate. Set latency and peak-load targets first, keep app compute for serving the UI, and write async code with recoverable state. Then let load tests and telemetry decide whether to scale up to a larger instance or out to more instances.

Should I scale up or scale out my Databricks App?

It depends on which limit the app hits first. Scale out by adding instances when requests arrive in bursts or a single-process app is bound to one core. Scale up to Large or XLarge when the app needs more memory, or when it runs several workers that can use extra cores.

What instance sizes does Databricks Apps offer?

Databricks Apps offers Medium (the default, up to 2 vCPUs and 6 GB), Large (up to 4 vCPUs and 12 GB) and XLarge (up to 12 vCPUs and 48 GB). Start on Medium and let a load test show which size your app needs.

How do I keep user sessions working when an app restarts or scales?

Split session state into soft state, which can be rebuilt, and hard state, which is stored durably in Lakebase or Unity Catalog tables. Databricks Apps keeps each user on the same instance on a best-effort basis, but restarts and scaling can still move a session, so any instance must be able to rebuild it from hard state.

How many Lakebase connections can a scaled app open?

With one pool per worker, the upper bound is instances × workers per instance × maximum pool size. For example, five instances with eight workers and a pool maximum of ten can open up to 400 connections. Compare that total with the database's documented limit, and leave headroom for deployments.

Ready to take your app from a few users to thousands? See Best practices for Databricks Apps and horizontal scaling for Databricks Apps in the documentation.

A practical guide to sharing data and AI assets on Databricks without building pipelines or exposing proprietary data

by Jordan Soldo

  • Databricks has three primary ways to share data and AI assets: OpenSharing, Clean Rooms, and Marketplace. Each one fits a different kind of relationship with the party on the other side.
  • Picking the wrong tool can waste an engineering sprint or expose data you meant to protect. These tools also remove the old work of copying data and building pipelines for every consumer.
  • Let the relationship decide how you share data: use OpenSharing for live, read-only access with a known recipient. Use Clean Rooms when partners want to combine data without exposing all of it. Use Marketplace to reach, or find, audiences you don't know yet.

The world of sharing has extended far past tables. We can now securely share all kinds of data and AI assets, from models to notebooks to AI agents, and the appetite to do so only keeps growing. While in the past, it may have been difficult to get just a table to or from a partnering business, these days it's easier than ever to provide access.

With this growing demand, we have seen three methods of sharing pop up in Databricks: OpenSharing, Clean Rooms, and Marketplace. With the emergence of these three, the question arises: “When do I use one over the other?” Picking the wrong one can cost you a wasted engineering sprint, or worse, expose data you meant to keep protected. In this blog, we'll dive into the three different sharing options and how they can apply to your business and your partnerships. As we'll see, the right choice usually comes down to one thing: the relationship you have with whoever is on the other side of the data.

First, we have OpenSharing, the simplest way to share data assets. Essentially, you create a share, associate assets with it, and provide access to that share to recipients. OpenSharing will handle the access, even if that recipient isn't on Databricks. This changes the paradigm as you no longer need to stand up pipelines to ship data to each consumer. Instead, consumers get direct read-only access to the original live asset once you've granted it, so what they see is always up to date.

Even popular BI tools like Power BI and Tableau can read directly from OpenShared tables. So a partner can directly connect their BI to the data you share with them.

You may have noticed I used the word “data assets." That is because you can share more than just tables with businesses outside your organization, including tables (Delta or Iceberg), Views, Volumes, Notebooks, UDFs, and even AI Models. This is also not limited to outside organizations; several businesses use OpenSharing to share data with different business units.

Across industries, we have seen businesses utilize or ingest data from partnered businesses via OpenSharing:

  • Retail: Businesses sharing point-of-sale data with their CPG suppliers
  • Healthcare: Hospital networks handing de-identified data to a named research partner
  • Manufacturing: sharing demand forecasts and inventory positions with their key suppliers

You might be thinking you could do this yourself by standing up a pipeline to share data out and managing credentials. And you would be correct, but the point of OpenSharing is to remove that overhead. You do not need to make copies of your data and spend unnecessary money. You share in minutes, and revoke just as fast.

Next, we have the Databricks Clean Rooms, which is much like it sounds: a sealed, neutral space where two or more businesses (up to ten) can bring their data together and run only the code every party has approved. Everyone benefits from the results, but no one ever sees another party's full underlying data. Let's say my company has proprietary data, and a business we partner with frequently has data they want to marry with ours to maximize value. Neither of us wants to share a full dataset, but we believe there is value in sharing snippets of data or joining our data on select fields. Instead of sending the full dataset over, we both share our table’s names and columns with each other and collaborate on authoring a notebook. For anything to run, we both have to give a thumbs-up of approval.

That, in essence, is how Clean Rooms operate. They let us collaborate with another business and intermingle data that is proprietary to each of us, while limiting what we share to only what we agreed to in that handshake. This is extremely common across a few industries:

  • Advertising and media: measuring campaign reach and audience overlap without exchanging entire customer lists
  • Healthcare: combining patient or clinical-trial data across organizations under strict privacy controls
  • Retail and CPG: matching loyalty and sell-through data to plan joint promotions

Reach for a clean room when combining data is valuable, but neither side wants to expose its full underlying data. The key difference is that, rather than giving the recipient direct access to the object itself, you only see the results of code that both sides have approved.

Last, we have the Databricks Marketplace. Think of it as a public storefront where you can share Files, Tables, Models, MCP (Model Context Protocol) Servers, Notebooks, Apps, and SaaS software. OpenSharing and Clean Rooms are options when you have an existing relationship with your customer. The Databricks Marketplace is about the ones you do not. It is an open exchange where data providers, software vendors, and technology partners publish offerings that any Databricks customer can discover, evaluate, and connect to directly from their workspace.

If you are a provider, it is a storefront that puts your assets in front of a broad audience. On the other side, if you are a consumer, you can find data and AI products to plug into your own work. Either way, what sets Marketplace apart is that it is public and discoverable: with OpenSharing and Clean Rooms, you already know who is on the other side, but on Marketplace, anyone can find your listing without you ever having met them.

Common examples of Marketplace:

  • A financial-data vendor monetizing market datasets
  • A weather forecasting service listing global weather datasets
  • A consultancy packaging an industry-specific ML model or Genie agent
  • A software vendor publishing a ready-to-run analytics app that customers launch in their own workspace
  • A SaaS vendor publishing an MCP Server that plugs into your own AI agents

Reach for Marketplace when you do not have a specific recipient in mind: you either want to be found, or you want to go find data and AI products yourself.

If you are still on the fence about which approach to use, let the relationship decide. If you already know exactly who should receive the data and you're comfortable sharing a read-only version, reach for OpenSharing. If you have a specific partner but neither side wants to expose its full underlying data, use a Clean Room. And if you don't have a specific recipient yet but want to be discovered, or you want to discover data and AI products yourself, that's Marketplace. Lastly, these are not mutually exclusive; the same business can use different tools for different relationships.

At the end of the day, these are all tools meant to enable your business and prevent slowdown from the traditional burdens of data sharing. So if you ever have customers asking for data, think about the relationship and match it to the right tool!
